title: I don’t want AI misuse to be impossible. I want it to be illogical.
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Matthews, drawing on work with more than twenty schools where student AI misuse came up every time, argues that misuse is a desire problem rather than a design problem. A student with a completion goal sees school as work to be finished, and for that student AI is the logical answer because the minimum dose of intellectual investment has fallen to almost nothing. A student with a formation goal understands that education shapes the person, so handing the work to a machine makes no sense. He cites James K.A. Smith on education as formation and says assessment redesign alone (handwritten essays, spoken tasks) only builds higher walls and teaches that the wall is the only reason to do the work. He answers the developmental objection by pointing to the gym, sport and music, where students already grasp that training cannot be outsourced. Filed as Ed-Tech because AI misuse in schools is the subject, though the argument is philosophical.
points: Matthews reframes AI misuse in schools as a problem of what students want rather than what tasks allow, so the aim is to make misuse illogical, not impossible.
A completion goal makes AI the rational choice because the minimum intellectual effort to finish a task has dropped to near zero.
Assessment redesign is described as a band-aid: higher walls protect conditions for learning but teach students the wall is the only reason to do the work.
Students already hold a formation view in the gym, sport and music, so the task is to turn that lens on their education.
The foundational principle is that the goal of education is to produce a person, not work.
quotes: A student with a formation goal doesn’t misuse AI because it just doesn’t make sense. Misusing AI can produce the work, but it cannot produce the person.

The minimum sufficient dose of intellectual investment has dropped to near zero. A prompt or two, a generic tool or a specialised one, and the task that was meant to occupy a week is finished in under a minute.
AI is the clear, logical, obvious answer to one particular question: how do I most effectively complete this task? If that is the question a student is asking, then AI is not the wrong answer.

What I want them to recognise is that they themselves are what’s being produced. “Will this be on the test?” and “Is this actually assessed?” stop functioning as the load-bearing questions of their education, because the test or the assessment was never the point of the thing in the first place.
Redesign operates on what a student can do, building higher and cleverer walls around the task. Formation operates on what a student wants, and want sits a long way beneath anything design can reach.

If all we ever do is build higher walls, we inadvertently teach students that the wall is the only reason to do the work at all. Remove the wall, as we eventually must, and we’ve removed the reason along with it.

A student knows perfectly well that paying a mate to lift their weights only grows their mate’s arms, because the point was never the weight that got moved. The point was the body being built, and that can’t be outsourced.
